claims.text: The target material is bulk equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework combines ab initio finite-temperature simulations, machine-learning adjustments informed by binary phase diagrams, and explicit modeling of oxygen defects.
The integrated framework will predict conductivity more accurately than approaches based on perfect, defect-free crystals.
Oxygen impurities produce defect states or local lattice distortions in the alloy.
Oxygen-induced defects and distortions modify electron or phonon scattering channels and thereby affect conductivity.
Quantum and defect scattering effects are prominent in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering and thermal disorder dominate conductivity behavior in the 300–1200 K regime.
Finite-temperature ab initio modeling can represent finite-temperature effects in refractory multi-principal-element alloys.
Machine learning based on binary-phase-diagram parameters can improve predictions for high-entropy alloys.
Binary-phase-diagram-informed machine learning can provide corrections to conductivity predictions.
The framework will capture low-temperature oxygen-induced scattering and high-temperature vibrational disorder.
Existing analytical models generally assume defect-free ideal crystals and omit oxygen-induced scattering and finite-temperature dynamics.
Existing analytical models overestimate conductivity or inaccurately reproduce its temperature dependence.
Predictions will agree with measurements within approximately 10–15% over 300–1200 K.
From 0–200 K, the predicted conductivity will show a discernible oxygen-enhanced-scattering trend relative to defect-free predictions.
The approach is intended to apply to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing around 1 wt.% oxygen at temperatures up to approximately 1200 K.
The approach is not established above the material's phase-stability limit.
A controlled specimen will be structurally characterized to determine oxygen distribution and defect density before conductivity-model comparison.
Deviation exceeding 15% from measurements across 300–1200 K will falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to obtain a discernible low-temperature difference from defect-free-model predictions will falsify the hypothesis.
